You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

def f(g):
    H,W=len(g),len(g[0])
    bg=max(set(x for r in g for x in r), key=lambda v: sum(r.count(v) for r in g))
    cells=[(i,j,g[i][j]) for i in range(H) for j in range(W) if g[i][j]!=bg]
    bycol={}
    for c,p in [(g[i][j],(i,j)) for i in range(H) for j in range(W) if g[i][j]!=bg]: bycol.setdefault(c,[]).append(p)
    out=[[bg]*W for _ in range(H)]
    def paint(i,j,v):
        if 0<=i<H and 0<=j<W and out[i][j]==bg: out[i][j]=v
    def reflect_beam(i,j,d0):
        # beam from (i,j) direction d0, traveling; reflects off any non-bg cell
        di,dj=d0; ii,jj=i+di,j+dj
        while True:
            if not (0<=ii<H and 0<=jj<W): return
            v=g[ii][jj]
            if v!=bg:
                # reflect: flip both components (reverse incoming diagonal)
                di2,dj2=-di,-dj
                ii,jj=i+di2,j+dj2  # continue from source cell with reversed direction? no—continue from the OBSTACLE
                ii,jj=ii+di2,jj+dj2
            elif (ii,jj) in set(cells) and g[ii][jj]==v:
                return  # absorbed by same color
            else:
                paint(ii,jj,v)
                ii+=di; jj+=dj
    for c,ps in bycol.items():
        if len(ps)==1: continue
        (a,b),(d,e)=ps[0],ps[-1]
        assert abs(a-d)==abs(b-e), ps
        di,dj=(1 if d>a else -1, 1 if e>b else -1)
        reflect_beam(a,b,(di,dj))
        reflect_beam(d,e,(-di,-dj))
    return out

import itertools,json
def f(g):
    H,W=len(g),len(g[0])
    bg=max(set(x for r in g for x in r), key=lambda v: sum(r.count(v) for r in g))
    out=[[bg]*W for _ in range(H)]
    def paint(i,j,v):
        if 0<=i<H and 0<=j<W and out[i][j]==bg: out[i][j]=v
    # same-color diagonal pairs emit beams toward each other; reflect off other colors (flip dc), stop at own color
    for c,ps in {g[i][j]:[(i,j) for i in range(H) for j in range(W) if g[i][j]==c} .items():
        if len(ps)<2: continue
        ps=list(ps)
        for p,q in itertools.combinations(ps,2):
            (r1,c1),(r2,c2)=p,q
            if abs(r1-r2)!=abs(c1-c2): continue
            di=(1 if r2>r1 else -1); dj=(1 if c2>c1 else -1)
            for start,d0 in [((r1,c1),(di,dj)),((r2,c2),(-di,-dj))]:
                i,j=start; sdi,sdj=d0
                while True:
                    ii,jj=i+sdi,j+sdj
                    if not(0<=ii<H and 0<=jj<W): break
                    ov=g[ii][jj]
                    if ov==bg:
                        paint(ii,jj,c); i,j=ii,jj; sdi,sdj=sdi+1 if False else sdi,sdj
                        # advance direction for next step manually below
                    elif ov==c:
                        break
                    else:
                        # reflect: flip dc; continue with obstacle's color? check demo2: painted 6 there (obstacle color)
                        nd=(sdi,-sdj); ni,nj=i+nd[0],j+nd[1]
                        if not(0<=ni<H and 0<=nj<W): break
                        paint(ni,nj,g[ii][jj]); i,j=ni,nj; sdi,sdj=nd; ii,jj=None,None
                        break
    return out
for k in ['Demo pair 2','Demo pair 3']:
    print(k, f(G[k+' input'])==G[k+' output'])

import os,re,json,itertools
def load():
    d=os.path.normpath(os.environ['RLM_SESSION_DIR'])
    t=open(d+'/../../sessions/'+os.path.basename(d)+'.jsonl').read().replace('\\n','\n'); G={}
    for m in re.finditer(r'(Demo pair \d+ (?:input|output)|Test input) \((\d+)x(\d+)\):\n',t):
        k,h,w=m[1],int(m[2]),int(m[3])
        rows=[r.split() for r in t[m.end():].split('\n')[:h]]
        if k not in G and all(len(r)==w and all(x.isdigit() for x in r) for r in rows):
            G[k]=[[int(x) for x in r] for r in rows]
    return G
G=load(); print(sorted(G))

Missing (0,7) and (3,4)! (3,4) is a 6 source. (0,7)? Why missing? Hmm — the 6 at (3,4) blocks it: cell (3,4) belongs to both lines. (0,7): hmm not filled. Wait diff for my earlier run said mine had extra 8 where exp has 6... Let me look carefully.

Demo 2: 1s at (1,6),(6,1). Diagonal i+j=7. Output 1-cells on that diag: (1,6),(2,5),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1). Missing (0,7) and (3,4). So the line through the two 1s spans between them plus one extension? Between (1,6) and (6,1): cells (1..6, 6..1): (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1) — but (3,4) is occupied by 6, so it stays 6? And (0,7) outside the span is also missing. Hmm. Maybe each 1 extends its line from just after itself toward the other 1: from (1,6) downward-right direction? (1,6)->(2,5)... going down-left. From (6,1) upward: (5,2),(4,3) then hits (3,4) which is 6 → stop. From (1,6) continuing up-right would be (0,7) — not filled. So each 1 extends only toward the other 1 along the shared diagonal. Interesting: like they "draw" the segment between the two same-color points, stopping at obstacles.

Check demo 3: 1s at (1,7),(7,1), diag sum 8. Output fills all of them including both endpoints: (1,7)..(7,1). That matches "segment between". And 6 single point unchanged. Good.

Demo 5: 1s at (2,2),(3,12),(11,11),(14,3). Output 1s: (2,2),(3,3),(4,4)...,(8,8),(10,10),(11,11),(14,3). So 1-line through (2,2)&(11,11)? They're on main diagonal d=i-j=0. Output fills (2,2)..(11,11) excluding (10,10)? wait (10,10) present yes. But (9,9) is a 6 source! (9,9) is 6 in input, so 1-line stops before it: fills up to (8,8) and resumes (10,10),(11,11). The other 1s (3,12),(14,3) unchanged; no pairs on a diagonal among them? (3,12): sum=15; (14,3): sum=17; i-j=-9 and 11. No pair shares diag. So those stay as single dots. Consistent with my earlier pairwise logic: pairs on same anti-diagonal (i+j const) get connected.

Wait but demo 5's 1-pair (2,2)-(11,11) is main diagonal (same i-j), not anti-diagonal. Hmm. My rule was anti-diagonal only. Need both diagonal directions. Demo 5's 6s: (1,8) alone on its anti-diag? out 6-cells: (1,8),(3,15),(4,14),(5,13),(6,12),(7,11),(8,10),(9,9),(10,8)...(14,4). So 6s connect (1,8) and (9,9): anti-diag sum 9 → fills (1,8)..(9,9). Then (9,9)..(14,4)? those have sums 18,11,... no. Let's see: (10,8),(11,7),(12,6),(13,5),(14,4): sum 18. That's a line through (9,9)? (9,9) sum 18! Yes main diagonal direction: from (9,9) going down-left to (14,4). And (14,13)? separate single dot. Hmm wait (14,13) has sum 27, no.

So each color connects pairs of points lying on a shared diagonal (either direction), filling cells between them, skipping/stop at other colors. In demo 4: 1s (3,1) and (9,7) — different diags. Out 1s: (3,1),(4,2),(6,4),(7,5),(9,7): fills between (3,1) and (9,7)? (4,2),(5,3)? (5,3) is a 6 source → stops there and resumes at (6,4)? After (4,2) next is (5,3)=6 obstacle; from 6 at (5,3)... hmm the resume: (6,4),(7,5) continuing direction down-right. So the line passes through the 6 obstacle? Like paint continues over other colors except stop at end? Actually (5,3) remains 6, and line continues beyond: (6,4),(7,5) then reaches (9,7)? gap at (8,6) which is a 6. Then continues? (8,6) is 6; (9,7) is endpoint. So effectively: fill entire diagonal path between the two 1s, skipping over cells occupied by other colors (those keep their color). Check demo 2 with this: (0,7) though—line between (1,6) and (6,1) doesn't include (0,7). OK.

But does the line extend past endpoints to grid edge if no blocking? Demo 5: 1s (2,2),(11,11) pair: fills (3,3)...(10,10) skipping nothing, and stops at both ends (doesn't extend to (1,-1)). Yes exactly segment.

Demo 4's 6-pairs: (2,9)&(5,3): diag sum 11 vs 8 — not aligned. i-j: -7 and 2. Anti: no. Hmm. Out 6s near there: (0,8),(1,7),(2,6),(3,5),(4,4),(5,3): these lie on i-j=-7: through (2,9). Fills up to (5,3) which is a 1?? no (5,3) is 6 in input. This is a segment from (2,9) going down-left until hitting (5,3), the other 6. But (5,3) and (2,9): dr=3,dc=-6 — not diagonal! Yet both endpoints are 6 and cells (3,5),(4,4) between. Hmm so connection isn't strictly diagonal.

Look again demo 4 output row0: (0,8)=6. (1,7),(2,6),(3,5),(4,4),(5,3)=6. That's diagonal i-j=-7 from (2,9) extending both ways: up-right (1,8)? but (1,8) is 5 in output (row1 "...565555" position 8=5). Hmm (0,8): i-j=-8. Row2 (2,6): i-j=-4? 2-6=-4. Let me recompute: cells listed: (0,8):r-c=-8; (1,7):-6; (2,6):-4; (3,5):-2; (4,4):0; (5,3):-2; (3,11):r-c=-8; (4,10):-6; (5,9):-4; (6,8):-2; (7,7):0; (8,6):-2; (9,5):-4; (10,4):-6; (11,3):-8; (12,2):-10; (13,1):-12; (14,0):-14. These alternate. So each 6 generates BOTH diagonal directions: from (5,3): up-right (4,4),(3,5) and down-left (6,2),(7,1),(8,0). From (2,9): down-left (3,8)? no—out (2,9),(3,11)? Hmm (3,11): r+c=14; (2,9): 11. Not same.

This is getting long. Perhaps simpler: each colored pixel extends anti-diagonals in all four directions until hitting another colored pixel, painting bg cells, stopping at colored pixels, and single-color pixels (no partner) still extend full length? Demo 4: 6 at (2,9): partners? none other 6 nearby. Output has (0,8),(1,7) above (2,9) — up-left direction; and presumably below: (3,8)? not in output... hmm (3,8) not present. Odd.

Alternatively maybe pairs of SAME COLOR anywhere (not necessarily diagonal) get connected by L-shaped or shortest path? Demo 4: 6 sources: (2,9),(5,3),(8,6),(13,4). Segment drawn: (0,8),(1,7),(2,6),(3,5),(4,4),(5,3),(3,11)? ...

Alternative reading: each source draws an X (both diagonals) until blocked, and when two same-color sources' lines meet they merge? Time budget. Let me think about what pattern outputs for 6 in demo 4 more carefully — draw coordinates:
Input 6s: A(2,9), B(5,3), C(8,6), D(13,4).
Output 6-cells besides inputs: (0,8),(1,7); (3,5),(4,4); (3,11),(4,10),(5,9),(6,8),(7,7)? no (7,7)... let me list all output 6s sorted: (0,8),(1,7),(2,6),(2,9),(3,5),(3,11),(4,4),(4,10),(5,3),(5,9),(6,2),(6,8),(7,1),(7,7),(8,0),(8,6),(9,5),(10,4),(11,3),(12,2),(13,1),(13,4),(14,0).

Note (7,7): appears in both lists: input has 1 at (9,7) and 6 at... (7,7) is added 6. Two lines cross at (7,7)? Line through (2,9),(5,3): i-j=-7... (7,7): i-j=0. No.

Hmm, notice structure: pairs (A(2,9),(5,3)): Δ=(3,-6). (B(5,3),(8,6)): Δ=(3,3). (C(8,6),(13,4)): Δ=(5,-2).

Idea: maybe each PAIR of same-color points defines a line with ANY slope, and output draws cells ON THAT LINE (including non-diagonal steps?) Only cells where step is diagonal-ish? B→C: (6,4)? not in output. Hmm.

Maybe instead: each source emits rays in all 4 diagonal directions, bouncing off edges/walls? Like billiards? Demo 4: 6 at (2,9): ray up-left: (1,8),(0,7)... but output has (1,7),(0,8) — not matching.

OK alternative approach: count: output 6 cells = 22. Maybe the rule relates to connecting each 6 to nearest same-color via king moves? Eh.

Time to try hypothesis H: for each pair of same-colored points, draw the line segment using Bresenham with any slope, keeping only cells close enough? (2,9)-(5,3): slope dr/dc=-0.5. Cells: (2,9),(3,8)? not present.

Hypothesis I: reflect. 1s (3,1),(9,7) in demo 4: difference (6,6) — diagonal i=j+2. Output fills (3,1),(4,2),(5,3)?? but (5,3) is 6. Output has (6,4),(7,5) then (9,7). So indeed: segment between the two 1s along i-j=2? (5,3) lies on it too. So fills (3,1)..(9,7) minus obstacles which retain their color. 

Now demo 5: 1s (2,2),(11,11): i-j=0. Fill (3,3)..(10,10) minus obstacles: (9,9) is 6 — but output shows (8,8) then (10,10), i.e., (9,9) stays 6. Good. Other 1s singletons unchanged.

6s demo 5: (1,8),(9,9): i+j=9? (1,8)=9 yes! Anti-diagonal sum 9: fill (2,7),(3,6)...? Those aren't in output. Hmm output 6s: (3,15),(4,14),...,(9,9) — that's anti-diag sum 18 through (9,9) and (14,4). And sum-11: (2,9),(3,8)? no wait output 6 at (2,9)? Yes (2,9) is input. (10,8): sum 18. So pair (9,9)-(14,13)? (14,13): sum 27. Hmm. Which 6-pairs are diagonal? (1,8)&(9,9): sum 9/18 no. (1,8)&(10,1): diff (9,-7) no. (10,1)&(14,13): no.

Output 6 lines: sum=9 [(1,8)] only; sum=11 [(10,1),(11,7)...] wait (10,1):sum 11. (11,7)? sum 18. Hmm earlier output listing: 6 at (10,8):sum 18. And sum=11: (2,9)? sum 11. (9,9)+(k,k) going down-left to (14,4)]. And (10,8),(11,7),(12,6),(13,5),(14,4)... wait that overlaps: (10,8) sum 18 yes! (14,4) sum 18 yes. So one line sum 18 from (9,9) to (14,4)? But (14,4) is not a 6 source! Where did it come from? It must connect two things... Hmm wait maybe (14,13) is on sum 27 and (14,4) on sum 18. Hmm.

Hold on, output 6 list again: (1,8),(3,15),(4,14),(5,13),(6,12),(7,11),(8,10),(9,9),(10,8),(11,7),(11,?)... let me recount from printed: (3,15),(4,14),(5,13),(6,12),(7,11),(8,10),(9,9),(10,8),(11,7),(12,6),(13,5),(14,4). Grid is 15x16, so (14,4) bottom row. Also up-right from (9,9): (8,10),(7,11)... those are on the same line! Wait (8,10),(7,11),(6,12),(5,13),(4,14),(3,15) — all sum 18, same line! Full line: from (3,15) to (14,4) passing through (9,9). Up-right part: (3,15)..(8,10); down-left part: (10,8)..(14,4). So 6 at (9,9) fills entire anti-diagonal i+j=18! Similarly (10,1): output has (10,1) only? sum 11: cells (2,9)? sum 11 — (2,9) is a 6 source! And (3,8)? not in output. Hmm. So (2,9),(10,1) same anti-diagonal sum 11: filled only between them? Cells between on sum 11: (3,8),(4,7),...(9,2),(10,1). Output: only (10,1) and (2,9). Not filled! Unless blocked... they'd need (9,2)...(3,8) — all bg in input? Input 6s elsewhere: none on that diagonal. Hmm.

Wait maybe pairs of same color don't both fill; maybe each source extends a diagonal toward the NEAREST same-color source, filling up to but excluding... For demo 5, 6 at (2,9) and (10,1) (sum 11): between them nothing filled — contradicts.

And 6 at (1,8): not extended: sum 9 line up-right: (0,9) absent; down-left (2,7) absent.

Hmm why stop at (10,10) after resuming? Because original segment between... the two 1s (2,2) and (11,11) define the segment; the segment is between the two source 1s! That fits demo 2: 1s (1,6),(6,1) fill segment excluding source cells... and (3,4) occupied by 6 stays 6 (sources keep color, and the drawing skips occupied cells, leaving them). Does it extend beyond endpoints? Demo 2: beyond (1,6) up-right: (0,7) — not drawn. Beyond (6,1) down-left: (7,0) — not drawn. So segment strictly between the two sources inclusive? But (3,4) inside segment is 6 and stays 6. Demo 3: 1s (1,7),(7,1), segment = whole thing; no obstacle. Demo 5: 1s (2,2),(11,11): segment excludes (9,9)=6 which keeps its color. Everything else on segment becomes 1. Matches!

Other 1s without partners (demo 5: (3,12),(14,3)) unchanged. Demo 4: 1s (3,1),(9,7): segment: (4,2),(5,3)? (5,3) is a 6 source → stays 6. Output has (6,4),(7,5). Anti-diagonals (i+j): (0,8)=8, (1,7)=8, (2,6)=8, (3,5)=8, (4,4)=8 — YES all sum 8! That's the segment through (5,3) (sum 8)! Extending the 1-pair? No wait that segment: which 6 sources on sum 8? Only (5,3). So a SINGLE 6 fills its own anti-diagonal entirely?! But earlier analysis said segment between two 6 sources. Hmm, now reconsider: maybe EVERY cell of a color, when paired with ANOTHER cell of same color anywhere on its diagonal (any distance), fills the FULL diagonal (through entire grid), and the pair (5,3),(8,6) case: (5,3) sum 8, (8,6) sum 14 — not paired. So (5,3)'s full anti-diagonal fill: cells (0,8),(1,7),(2,6),(3,5),(4,4),(5,3),(6,2),(7,1),(8,0) — ALL IN OUTPUT! ✓✓✓

Then demo 5's 6 at (9,9): full anti-diagonal sum 18 — all present ✓ (also (3,15)...(8,10) up-right and (10,8)..(14,4) down-left). So single 6 sources fill entire anti-diagonals?? Output: (0,7)? row0: "86888888888" col1=6. (0,7)=8! Not 6. Hmm contradiction.

Unless each color forms one combined object: maybe each color's cells, when projected, get connected... Look at demo 4's 1s: (3,1),(9,7) differ by (6,6) — main diagonal! Demo 5's 1s: (2,2),(11,11) on main diagonal i-j=0 — filled between with 6 at (9,9) skipped. Other 1s (3,12),(14,3): no partner, unchanged.

Demo 2's 1s: (1,6),(6,1) anti-diagonal i+j=7 — filled between, skipping 6 at (3,4). But why not extended beyond? Because segment between pair. Demo 3: 1s (1,7),(7,1) anti-diagonal sum 8 — fully filled.

So rule: same-color pairs that lie on a common diagonal (either orientation) → fill segment between them (all bg cells on that segment become that color; other-color cells on the segment stay). Single-cell colors stay. But demo 4's 6s produced many more segments than I expected. 6 sources: (2,9),(5,3),(8,6),(13,4). Pairs sharing a diagonal: (5,3)&(8,6) share main diag i-j=2 → segment (6,4),(7,5) — those are 1s anyway. (5,3) anti-diag sum 8 contains no other 6, so it fills wholly. But then demo 2's 6 at (3,4) sum 7 would fill wholly including (0,7),(7,0) — it didn't. Unless filling happens only between two same-color cells of that color (the pair anchors the segment, extended to grid edges?). Demo 2: 6 pair? only one 6. Hmm.

New idea: maybe every color cell extends along BOTH diagonals fully, but cells are overwritten by... priority order: later-drawn colors overwrite? Demo 2: 1s drawn first fill seg (1,6)-(6,1) on sum 7, skipping (3,4)? then 6 at (3,4) fills anti-diag sum 7 fully? That would overwrite the 1s back to 6. Output has 1s there. Order matters: process 6s then 1s? 6 at (3,4) fills anti-diag fully → (0,7),(1,6),(2,5),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1),(7,0) become 6; then 1s processed: 1 pair (1,6),(6,1) fills sum-7 segment → overwrites back to 1? then output would be all 1s on that diagonal. No.

OK alternative: think of it as each color fills the full diagonal(s) passing through ITS cells, but only the diagonal containing ≥2 of its cells gets filled fully; diagonals with a single cell... in demo 2, 6 has one cell: its anti-diag sum 7 has another 6? no. Hmm but (0,1)...(7,8) line sum... (3,4) main-diag i-j=-1: only one 6 there too. Output 6s on i-j=-1: (0,1),(1,2),(2,3) — yes! that's the main diagonal through (3,4)! (2,9): main d=-7, anti s=11 — no partner on either diagonal. (13,4): main d=9, anti s=17 — no partner. So rule: a color cell extends along both diagonals UNLESS isolated (has no same-color neighbor on a diagonal)? But then (5,3)&(8,6) pair: each fills full diagonals through themselves? But s=8 and s=14 were fully filled, and main d=2 between them (6,4),(7,5) are 1s — stayed 1. Hmm but why weren't (6,4),(7,5) converted to 6? Because 1s already there (1-segment wins / 1 processed later?). Priority: maybe each color claims cells on its diagonals, and conflicts resolved by... the segment rule for 1s overrides?

Actually maybe simpler unified rule: each color draws its full diagonals EXCEPT cells belonging to another color's claimed segment? Demo 4: 6 at (5,3): anti-diag s=8 fully filled → (0,8),(1,7),(2,6),(3,5),(4,4),(6,2),(7,1),(8,0) ✓. 6 at (8,6): anti-diag s=14 fully → (3,11)..(14,0) ✓. 6 at (2,9): anti s=11 AND main d=-7 fully?
